# How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning

###### Abstract.

Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are
restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which
trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy
distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own
rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and
on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference
solution. We ask how much of that reference signal is actually
necessary.

We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for
multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student
itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short
critique of that step. We truncate the student’s trajectory immediately
before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen
copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that
hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under
reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient.

We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial
reasoning benchmark that evaluates models on their ability to derive
core formula inputs from realistic financial scenarios via accounting
conventions and reasoning. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a
generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD’s entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain
over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, consistent with
most of that gain coming from where the supervision is applied rather
than hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be
stronger than the model receiving it—hints from same-family
GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly $`6\times`$ the parameters, yield no materially
greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches
on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy
while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on
MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no
material regression.

###### Keywords: 

knowledge distillation, self-distillation, on-policy distillation,
financial reasoning, large language models, post-training

## 1. Introduction

Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in the financial sector requires
careful balancing of performance and regulatory compliance.

The first compliance requirement is data residency. Customer records,
positions, and internal analyses frequently cannot leave institutional
infrastructure, which rules out API access to frontier models and
confines deployment to open-weight models served on-premise. Latency and
hardware budgets only tighten this further.

The second is behavioral assurance. A model used in an advisory or
analytical capacity is subject to institutional obligations around
disclosure, fiduciary care, and the handling of client information.
Post-training cannot be allowed to silently erode the behaviors that
make a model acceptable to deploy; however, domain fine-tuning is known
to degrade instruction-following and other post-trained behaviors
acquired during alignment ([Lu and Thinking Machines Lab,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)).

Data residency pushes practitioners toward small, open-weight models.
However, these models underperform on exactly the multi-step
quantitative reasoning that financial analysis demands, unless they are
given the fine-tuning that can compromise behavioral assurance. We
examine methods for rectifying this.

One of the easiest ways to close capability gaps is distillation, and
recent work has converged on on-policy distillation (OPD): sample
trajectories from the student, then have a teacher score each token of
those trajectories, typically via per-token reverse KL
divergence ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib10)).
Grounding supervision in student-generated states avoids the exposure
bias that afflicts training on teacher trajectories, and supplies a much
denser signal than outcome-based reinforcement learning. On-policy
self-distillation (OPSD) ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) removes the
external teacher by using the student itself, granted privileged
information, as its own teacher.

HINT-SD ([Yeo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) sharpens this further for
long-horizon agents, applying feedback-conditioned distillation only at
the failure-relevant turns rather than uniformly across the failed
trajectory.

This paper asks how much privileged information a self-distillation
teacher actually needs, and whether the resulting method is a practical
post-training recipe under the constraints above (increasing performance
while maintaining compliance and cost-effectiveness).

Our contributions are as follows:

1.  (1)
    We show that replacing the full hint with a fixed generic-feedback
    control does not materially degrade any of the three metrics, and
    matches the gain over base (+3.36 pp accuracy, vs Fin-SD’s +3.03).
    This leads us to hypothesize that problem-specific guidance is
    unnecessary once the mistake is properly localized.
2.  (2)
    Consistent with this, the model writing the hint does not need to be
    stronger than the model receiving it. On a corpus where
    non-arithmetic failures are dominated by convention selection, a 20B
    model is able to localize the error with the ground-truth answer in
    hand well enough that swapping out the hint writer for a stronger
    model with roughly $`6\times`$ the parameters does not make a
    significant difference in accuracy.
3.  (3)
    We present Fin-SD, a hindsight self-distillation recipe for
    multi-step finance reasoning. Fin-SD localizes the first faulty
    clause of a failed reasoning trajectory using the student’s own
    weights, truncates there, and distills a hint-conditioned frozen
    copy of the student into the student under reverse KL over a
    100-token rollout.

    ![Refer to caption](2610.36082v1/fig1.png)
    Figure 1. Overview of Fin-SD. The student is sampled on a training
    problem and judged against the ground truth. On failures, a frozen
    copy of the student receives the query, the failing trajectory, and
    the answer, and returns the first faulty step $`k`$, a short
    critique $`h`$, and an error type; pure arithmetic slips are dropped
    without a gradient. The trajectory is truncated immediately _before_
    k, so both policies condition on the on-policy prefix before the
    localized error, with the frozen teacher also receiving $`h`$. The
    student minimizes the per-token KL between the two next-token
    distributions over an L = 100 rollout. At each epoch boundary, the
    failure set is re-mined and the teacher re-frozen.

4.  (4)
    We show that a hint matches a full solution on accuracy, at lower
    cost. Comparing Fin-SD against OPSD, we find that it matches OPSD’s
    accuracy (72.19% for Fin-SD vs OPSD’s 70.42%), and Fin-SD generates
    9.5% fewer tokens at evaluation and is directionally more reliable
    on in-budget completion rate ($`+2.44`$ pp).
5.  (5)
    We demonstrate that the distillation process does not observably
    hurt compliance and general reasoning, reporting MMLU-Pro ([Wang
    et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) and FinTrust ([Hu et al.,
    2025](#bib.bib7)) performance for a model trained with Fin-SD.
6.  (6)
    We construct a corpus of difficult, multi-step financial reasoning
    problems from the FinanceReasoning function library ([Tang et al.,
    2025](#bib.bib13)). Rather than relying on explicit parameters, each
    problem presents a realistic market, timeline, or corporate
    accounting scenario requiring the user to apply strict financial
    definitions and conventions to derive key inputs. These derived
    inputs feed into a core financial function to yield an intermediate
    metric, which is then mapped to a single, unambiguous, and easily
    verifiable final numerical answer. This distinguishes it from
    benchmarks that assess information extraction or simple formula
    application as well as rubric-based benchmarks.

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1. From offline to on-policy distillation

Classical knowledge distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s
output distribution on a fixed dataset ([Hinton et al.,
2015](#bib.bib6)), with sequence-level variants training on
teacher-generated outputs ([Kim and Rush, 2016](#bib.bib9)). Both are
off-policy: the contexts seen in training are the teacher’s, not the
student’s. On long generations this produces compounding error, since
the student is never trained on recovery from its own mistakes.

On-policy distillation addresses this by sampling rollouts from the
student and evaluating the teacher on student-visited prefixes.
GKD ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) introduced the formulation for
autoregressive LMs and analyzed the choice of divergence; MiniLLM ([Gu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) argued for reverse KL on the grounds that its
mode-seeking behavior prevents the student from spreading mass over
regions the teacher considers unlikely; Lu and Thinking Machines
Lab ([Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib10)) give a practical
recipe using per-token reverse KL as a policy-gradient advantage, and
note that because no completed rollout is needed to compute the signal,
partial rollouts suffice—a property we exploit.

### 2.2. Self-distillation and privileged context

Context distillation ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib12)) trains a model
using a context-augmented version of itself as a teacher, internalizing
privileged information so it can be reproduced without context at
inference. Because the teacher and student share weights, this avoids
inheriting an external model’s artifacts (e.g., verbosity or refusal
behaviors).

Zhao et al. ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) instantiate this idea
directly for reasoning as on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). The
teacher policy conditions on privileged information (a verified
reference solution) while the student policy sees only the question, and
training minimizes the per-token divergence between the two
distributions along the student’s own rollouts. They report superior
token efficiency relative to reinforcement learning (RL) methods on
mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

HINT-SD ([Yeo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) combines this with targeted
supervision for long-horizon agents. Its observation is that in a failed
trajectory most turns are already successful or neutral, so distilling
uniformly across the trajectory spends the signal on positions that need
no correction; it therefore uses hindsight over the complete trajectory
to select failure-relevant action spans and applies feedback-conditioned
distillation only there. It reports gains over RL and full-trajectory
distillation on multi-step tool use benchmarks.

Our work adapts this to a different domain. Where HINT-SD operates over
multi-turn action spans in agentic environments, we operate over
reasoning steps within a single chain of thought, localizing to the
first clause at which the derivation goes wrong.

### 2.3. Financial reasoning benchmarks

Financial reasoning benchmarks have historically emphasized sentiment
and classification or extractive question answering over filings ([Islam
et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)). FinQA ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib4)) and
TAT-QA ([Zhu et al., 2021](#bib.bib17)) introduced numerical reasoning
over hybrid table-and-text contexts, but individual questions typically
require few arithmetic operations and present necessary quantities
explicitly.

Crucially, existing benchmarks bypass the critical step of using
financial logic to construct function inputs rather than merely
extracting explicitly stated variables. Our training corpus is
structured explicitly around this challenge.

FinanceReasoning ([Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)) is the closest
existing fit: its Hard subset comprises 238 problems requiring the
composition of multiple financial formulas, with Python-formatted
solutions and precise answers, and it releases a library of 3,133
financial functions. We use both—the function library to seed corpus
construction, and the Hard subset for evaluation.

For behavioral evaluation we use FinTrust ([Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)), which assesses seven compliance dimensions in
financial contexts.

### 2.4. Choice of divergence

The direction of the KL objective remains contested. OPSD ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)) finds forward KL works best due to its coverage and
stability; MiniLLM ([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) and OPD ([Lu and
Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib10)) favor reverse KL for
mode-seeking behavior, and HINT-SD ([Yeo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15))
follows suit. Fin-SD implements reverse KL, and we ablate against
forward KL
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2. Reverse direction outperforms forward ‣ 6. Ablations ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")).

## 3. Method

We consider a student policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ that produces incorrect
final answers on some subset of multi-step reasoning problems. Fin-SD
localizes the first point of failure in the student’s own trajectory,
conditions a teacher on a targeted critique at that point, and distills
the teacher’s next-step distribution into the student over a short
rollout.

### 3.1. Preliminaries and notation

Let $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x^{(i)},y^{*(i)})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}`$ be a
corpus of reasoning problems, where $`x`$ is a natural-language query
and $`y^{*}`$ a ground-truth answer. A policy $`\pi`$ maps a context to
a distribution over vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$ and induces trajectories
$`\tau=(t_{1},\dots,t_{N})`$, $`t_{j}\in\mathcal{V}`$, sampled
autoregressively. Write $`\tau_{<k}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{k-1})`$ and
$`\tau_{a:b}=(t_{a},\dots,t_{b})`$.

Three policies are involved, all of which are the student in Fin-SD:

Student ($`\pi_{\theta}`$)::  
the model being optimized. In all experiments this is
GPT-OSS-20B ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib11)).

Teacher ($`\pi_{\phi}`$)::  
a frozen copy of the student’s own weights, prompted with an additional
hint. The teacher is a context-augmented instantiation of the student,
not a separate model. We re-freeze it at each epoch boundary: during
epoch $`e`$, $`\phi=\theta^{(e-1)}`$, the student’s weights at the end
of the previous epoch. The distillation target therefore improves as the
student does, rather than remaining pinned to the initialization.

Hint model ($`\pi_{H}`$)::  
a frozen model used only for error localization and critique generation.
It is not distilled from, and therefore does not contribute a gradient.
In Fin-SD it is the frozen teacher’s own weights (self); we ablate
against GPT-OSS-120B (120b) in
Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1. Self-written hints match those of a larger same-family model ‣ 6. Ablations ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning").

Because $`\pi_{\phi}`$ and $`\pi_{\theta}`$ share weights and differ
only in the context they receive, the method is a form of context
distillation ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib12)): the aim is to
internalize the behavior the hint induces, so that it is reproduced
without the hint at inference.

### 3.2. Error localization and hint synthesis

Given a problem $`(x,y^{*})`$ on which the student fails
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Financial reasoning corpus ‣ 4. Experimental Setup ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")),
let $`\tau_{\mathrm{stud}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$ be the failing
trajectory. The hint model receives $`(x,\tau_{\mathrm{stud}},y^{*})`$
and returns

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

             ``` math
             (k,h,type)\sim\pi_{H}(\cdot\mid x,\tau_{\mathrm{stud}},y^{*}),
             ```                                                             |     |

where $`k`$ is the first token¹¹ 1 Because models struggle to return
exact token positions, we have the model return a quote with the
erroneous clause repeated verbatim, which is then indexed to a character
position for truncation. at which the trajectory departs from a valid
solution path, $`h`$ is a short natural-language critique describing the
departure, and $`type`$ is a classification of whether the error is
arithmetic or conceptual. The critique names, for example, the
convention the solver should have recognized or the correct way to apply
a critical concept, and takes the form “Your logic diverges when $`X`$…
Assume $`Y`$.” The informational content of $`h`$ turns out to be
largely dispensable; we isolate it in
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. A vague hint matches a targeted critique ‣ 5. Results ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning").

Failures whose only error is arithmetic carry no useful signal about
reasoning, and in practice would be avoided at the harness level with a
calculator tool. We therefore have $`\pi_{H}`$ additionally classify
each failure as a reasoning error or an arithmetic/rounding slip, and
suppress the weight update for the latter. Such items still count as
incorrect in all reported accuracies; only the gradient is withheld. An
informal audit of the classifier shows that it achieves 96% accuracy (48
out of 50 items correct).

### 3.3. Prefix grounding and teacher augmentation

We truncate the student trajectory immediately before the localized
error, yielding prefix $`\tau_{<k}`$. Both policies are conditioned on
this same prefix; only the teacher additionally receives the hint:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (2) |     |

````math
I_{\mathrm{stud}}=[x;\tau_{<k}],\qquad I_{\mathrm{teach}}=[x;\tau_{<k};h].
``` |  |

The prefix is drawn from the student’s own generation, so the contexts
on which the student is trained lie in its native distribution.

### 3.4. Distillation objective

We roll out $`L=100`$ tokens from the student,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
\tau_{\mathrm{roll}}=(t_{k},\dots,t_{k+L-1})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid I_{\mathrm{stud}}),
``` |  |

and align the student’s next-token distributions to the teacher’s along
this rollout. Writing
$`c_{j}^{\mathrm{stud}}=[I_{\mathrm{stud}};\tau_{k:j-1}]`$ and
$`c_{j}^{\mathrm{teach}}=[I_{\mathrm{teach}};\tau_{k:j-1}]`$ for the two
contexts at position $`j`$, and $`\mathcal{F}`$ as the set of localized
failures obtained by applying Eq. (1) to $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}`$
and discarding arithmetic slips, Fin-SD minimizes the reverse KL,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RKL}}(\theta)=\\
\mathbb{E}_{(x,\tau_{<k},h)\sim\mathcal{F}}\!\left[\sum_{j=k}^{k+L-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{j}^{\mathrm{stud}})\,\big\|\,\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid c_{j}^{\mathrm{teach}})\right)\right]
``` |  |

where $`D_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ is taken over the full vocabulary at each
position and the teacher’s distribution is treated as a constant target.
Only the $`L`$ rollout positions contribute loss; the prefix is masked
out.

1: corpus $`\mathcal{D}`$, student $`\pi_{\theta}`$, hint model
$`\pi_{H}`$, rollout length $`L`$, direction
$`d\in\{\mathrm{FKL},\mathrm{RKL}\}`$, accumulation steps $`A`$

2: updated student $`\pi_{\theta}`$

3: for $`\mathit{epoch}=1\dots E`$ do

4:   $`\phi\leftarrow\theta`$ $`\triangleright`$ re-freeze teacher

5:   $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

6:   for $`(x,y^{\star})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$ do
$`\triangleright`$ failure mining

7:    $`\tau_{\mathrm{stud}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$

8:    if
$`\textsc{Judge}(\textsc{Extract}(\tau_{\mathrm{stud}}),y^{\star})`$ is
incorrect then

9:
      $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}\cup\{(x,y^{\star},\tau_{\mathrm{stud}})\}`$

10:    end if

11:   end for

12:   $`g\leftarrow\mathbf{0}`$,   $`a\leftarrow 0`$ $`\triangleright`$
grad buffer, accumulation counter

13:   for
$`(x,y^{\star},\tau_{\mathrm{stud}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}`$ do

14:
   $`(k,h,\mathit{type})\sim\pi_{H}(\cdot\mid x,\tau_{\mathrm{stud}},y^{\star})`$

15:    if $`\mathit{type}=\textsc{arith\_slip}`$ then

17:    end if

19:    $`I_{\mathrm{teach}}\leftarrow[x;\tau_{<k};h]`$

20:

  $`|\tau_{\mathrm{roll}}|=L`$

21:    $`\mathcal{L}(\theta)\leftarrow\sum_{j}D_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ under
direction $`d`$, teacher $`\pi_{\phi}`$ on $`I_{\mathrm{teach}}`$,
student $`\pi_{\theta}`$ on $`I_{\mathrm{stud}}`$

22:    $`g\leftarrow g+\tfrac{1}{A}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)`$
$`\triangleright`$ accumulate scaled grad

23:    $`a\leftarrow a+1`$

24:    if $`a=A`$ then $`\triangleright`$ optimizer step every $`A`$
contributing examples

25:       $`\theta\leftarrow\textsc{AdamW-step}(\theta,g)`$

26:       $`g\leftarrow\mathbf{0}`$,   $`a\leftarrow 0`$

27:    end if

28:   end for

29:   if $`a>0`$ then $`\triangleright`$ flush partial batch

30:
   $`\theta\leftarrow\textsc{AdamW-step}\!\left(\theta,\tfrac{A}{a}\,g\right)`$

31:    $`g\leftarrow\mathbf{0}`$,   $`a\leftarrow 0`$

32:   end if

33:   evaluate on $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}`$

34: end for

35: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$

Algorithm 1 Fin-SD

Fin-SD sets $`\pi_{H}=\pi_{\phi}`$, $`d=\mathrm{RKL}`$, and $`L=100`$ in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.5. Additional notes ‣ 3. Method ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning");
the ablations of
Section [6](#S6 "6. Ablations ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")
isolate these three arguments.

Two properties follow from the loop structure:

1.  (1)
    The failure set is recomputed each epoch, so the training
    distribution tracks the student’s current weaknesses rather than
    being fixed at initialization.
2.  (2)
    Because the teacher is re-frozen alongside it, the method is
    iterative self-distillation with a hint, not distillation from a
    fixed initial checkpoint.

## 4. Experimental Setup

### 4.1. Financial reasoning corpus

#### Function curation.

We seed from the library of 3,133 Python-formatted financial functions
released with FinanceReasoning ([Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)). To
remove trivial operations, each function is graded on an 8-point
difficulty scale by an LLM grader (GPT-OSS-120B); we retain functions
scoring $`\geq 3`$. Retained functions pass to a viability judge
(DeepSeek-V4-Flash) verifying that each can support a word problem with
a single correct answer, yielding 295 formulas.

#### Problem generation.

For each formula, we synthesize context-rich, multi-step financial
reasoning problems using GPT-5.5. The design target is a problem where
key inputs are intentionally not specified directly, but must instead be
derived from standard finance conventions, market scenarios, or
financial statements. Each synthesized problem is structured into three
distinct phases:

1.  (1)
    Input Derivation: The user must analyze realistic financial
    scenarios, timelines, or balance sheet data to calculate the exact
    inputs required for the target formula based on standard industry
    definitions.
2.  (2)
    Core Function Execution: The derived inputs are evaluated through
    the target financial function to obtain an intermediate financial
    metric.
3.  (3)
    Verifiable Closing Mechanism: The intermediate metric is applied to
    a domain-native endpoint, such as comparing internal rate of return
    against a firm’s threshold or determining a precise dollar-value
    valuation impact.

We then perform a critique pass using Claude Fable 5, removing
contradictory premises and quantities that are truly underdetermined.
This focuses the corpus on tasks and ambiguity that a competent analyst
could confidently resolve.

All items were manually reviewed for logical validity and for the
existence of a unique correct answer under correct convention
application.
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Function curation. ‣ 4.1. Financial reasoning corpus ‣ 4. Experimental Setup ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")
shows a single item carried through all three phases, together with the
supervision Fin-SD applies to it. The final set contains 220 problems,
split 80/20 for training and validation.

While we utilize external LLMs to generate synthetic data for training,
in practice, the training corpus would be made up of on-premise data,
and so this phase does not strictly require an external model.

#### Failure mining.

Training instances are the subset on which the student fails. For each
$`(x,y^{*})`$ we sample
$`\tau_{\mathrm{stud}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$ and compare the
extracted answer to $`y^{*}`$ using an LLM equivalence judge
(DeepSeek-V4-Flash) tolerant of formatting and rounding differences (in
deployment, a well-designed deterministic parser would suffice as well).
Correct instances are discarded; the remainder form
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}`$, the input to
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.5. Additional notes ‣ 3. Method ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning").
We further filter this by excluding problems that the student is unable
to output an answer to within the token budget, as they may be too
difficult for the student at first. This reduces the potential training
set to around 60 questions per epoch, with the student gradually moving
to harder questions over time. Of these 60, around 35 are arithmetic
errors, so the final training set is roughly 25 problems per epoch.

### 4.2. Training configuration

We use GPT-OSS-20B ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib11)) as the student,
fine-tune with all-linear LoRA, and optimize it with AdamW. We select
the epoch with the highest in-distribution validation accuracy (this
same treatment applies to the OPSD and SFT baselines) and report
held-out accuracy on FinanceReasoning.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Training configuration ‣ 4. Experimental Setup ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")
lists the full configuration.

|                                |                                          |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Setting                        | Value                                    |
| *Model and optimization*       |                                          |
| Student model                  | GPT-OSS-20B ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib11)) |
| Student model effort           | Medium                                   |
| LoRA attention $`r`$           | $`64`$                                   |
| LoRA $`\alpha`$                | $`128`$                                  |
| LoRA expert $`r`$              | $`8`$                                    |
| Optimizer                      | AdamW                                    |
| Learning rate                  | $`2\times 10^{-5}`$                      |
| LR schedule                    | Cosine                                   |
| Warmup steps                   | $`15`$                                   |
| $`\beta_{2}`$                  | $`0.95`$                                 |
| Weight decay                   | $`0.0`$                                  |
| Gradient clipping              | $`1.0`$                                  |
| *Batching and data*            |                                          |
| Effective batch size           | $`16`$                                   |
| Train/validation split         | $`0.8/0.2`$                              |
| Epochs                         | $`10`$                                   |
| Reasoning rollout cap          | $`8192`$ tokens                          |
| *Fin-SD settings*              |                                          |
| Hint writer $`\pi_{H}`$        | self (frozen teacher)                    |
| KL direction $`d`$             | Reverse                                  |
| Distillation rollout cap $`L`$ | $`100`$ tokens                           |

Table 1. Student fine-tuning hyperparameters.

### 4.3. Evaluation and statistics

We evaluate on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset ([Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)), which is comprised of 238 multi-step finance
problems. We report accuracy (fraction solved), in-budget completion
rate (fraction of attempts that adhere to the 8192-token budget,
hereafter simply completion rate), and total tokens (cumulative
generation over the full evaluation).

We compare Fin-SD against three baselines—OPSD, SFT on reference
solutions, and the base GPT-OSS-20B, and we ablate hint content, hint
writer, KL direction, and rollout length. Fin-SD is trained under five
seeds (7, 42, 72, 2, 27), as is each ablation cell and OPSD; SFT is
trained under three seeds (7, 42, 72), and the base model is evaluated
under five independent runs. All runs are served at BF16 precision and
share the identical 238-problem set. We report means over seeds with
sample standard deviations and $`t`$-based 95% confidence intervals.

#### Sources of run-to-run variation.

Decoding temperature is 0.0, so the spread across runs is not sampling
variance. Sources of variation include training seeds, inference
non-determinism, and LLM-as-judge. The latter two are measurement noise
rather than model training variance.

Beyond the target domain we report MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)) for general reasoning and FinTrust ([Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)) for compliance. Both were evaluated on Fin-SD as
single runs.

## 5. Results

| Configuration | $`n`$ | Accuracy (%) | 95% CI | Completion rate (%) | 95% CI | Tokens (k) | 95% CI |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Fin-SD | 5 | $`\mathbf{72.19\pm 1.79}`$ | $`[70.0,\,74.4]`$ | $`\mathbf{92.19\pm 1.96}`$ | $`[89.8,\,94.6]`$ | $`\mathbf{508.5\pm 26.5}`$ | $`[476,\,541]`$ |
| OPSD (full solution) | 5 | $`70.42\pm 1.64`$ | $`[68.4,\,72.5]`$ | $`89.75\pm 1.35`$ | $`[88.1,\,91.4]`$ | $`562.1\pm 17.0`$ | $`[541,\,583]`$ |
| Base | 5 | $`69.16\pm 1.85`$ | $`[66.9,\,71.5]`$ | $`91.18\pm 1.95`$ | $`[88.8,\,93.6]`$ | $`525.8\pm 13.6`$ | $`[509,\,543]`$ |
| SFT | 3 | $`62.46\pm 3.50`$ | $`[53.8,\,71.2]`$ | $`99.02\pm 0.24`$ | $`[98.4,\,99.6]`$ | $`228.9\pm 3.9`$ | $`[219,\,239]`$ |

Table 2. Fin-SD against the three baselines. Mean $`\pm`$ SD over seeds,
with 95% confidence intervals.

### 5.1. Fin-SD improves over the base model

Fin-SD improves accuracy over base by $`3.03`$ pp (72.19% vs 69.16%),
raises completion rate by $`1.01`$ pp (92.19% vs 91.18%), and reduces
token consumption by 17.3k, or 3.3% (508.5k vs 525.8k).

### 5.2. Hints match full reference solutions at lower cost

Fin-SD reaches 72.19% against OPSD’s 70.42%, reduces token spend by
53.6k tokens, or 9.5% (508.5k vs 562.1k), and gains $`2.44`$ pp over
OPSD (92.19% vs 89.75%). It greatly improves over SFT, which is
ineffective here.

The interpretation is that a hint carries enough of the reference
solution’s signal to match it on task accuracy, while inducing a shorter
solution style.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3. Accuracy relative to the base model on the FinanceReasoning
Hard subset, including baselines and ablations. Points are mean
differences in percentage points; bars are $`t`$-based 95% confidence
intervals. All configurations are $`n=5`$ seeds except SFT ($`n=3`$);
base is $`n=5`$ independent runs. The SFT interval extends to $`-16.10`$
and is clipped at the axis limit (arrow).

### 5.3. A vague hint matches a targeted critique

Fin-SD uses informative hints: the critique is of the form “Your logic
diverges when $`X`$… Assume $`Y`$.” To test how much of Fin-SD’s benefit
comes from that content rather than from the machinery around it, we
replace $`h`$ with a fixed generic-feedback string—“Your mistake is
conceptual”, so that the placebo carries no problem-specific
information. Everything else is held constant.

The placebo does not underperform the full hint on any metric. Accuracy
is 72.52%, above Fin-SD by $`0.33`$ pp
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2. Hints match full reference solutions at lower cost ‣ 5. Results ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning"));
completion rate is higher by $`0.17`$ pp and token count lower by 4.7k.
All three gaps sit well inside the seed spread. Relative to base, the
placebo runs show no significant degradation: $`+3.36`$ pp accuracy,
$`+1.18`$ pp completion rate, and 22.0k fewer tokens.

This is consistent with the gains reported above being driven
predominantly by *where* the supervision is applied rather than by
*what* the critique says, assuming a sufficiently knowledgeable
student/base model. Truncating at $`k`$ returns the student to the
on-policy prefix before the localized error and concentrates the whole
distillation budget at the position where the derivation actually goes
wrong.

### 5.4. General capability and compliance

An important post-training constraint in highly regulated fields is that
it cannot degrade compliance or general reasoning. We report two
out-of-domain evaluations of Fin-SD.

#### MMLU-Pro.

For general reasoning, we evaluate on the MMLU-Pro benchmark, a large
evaluation suite comprised of just over 12,000 questions spanning a
variety of fields. To ensure appropriate out-of-domain evaluation, we
exclude the business and economics fields, reducing the benchmark to
just over 10,000 questions. We find that general reasoning performance
is near-identical, as is execution rate and mean tokens.

|                      |           |           |              |
|----------------------|-----------|-----------|--------------|
|                      | Base      | Fin-SD    | $`\Delta`$   |
| Overall accuracy (%) | $`68.91`$ | $`68.34`$ | $`-0.57`$ pp |
| Execution rate (%)   | $`98.56`$ | $`98.77`$ | $`+0.21`$ pp |
| Mean tokens          | 1,742     | 1,692     | $`-2.87\%`$  |

Table 3. MMLU-Pro.

The slight drop in overall accuracy is primarily driven by a 5.47 pp
drop in chemistry, with all other categories moving less than 2% in
either direction. We theorize that this is due to the significant number
of semantic collisions between finance and chemistry, e.g. yield,
concentration, etc.

#### FinTrust.

We evaluate fourteen metrics across the FinTrust compliance benchmark’s
seven dimensions: trustfulness, robustness, safety, fairness, privacy,
transparency, and knowledge discovery.

| Dimension / metric | Base | Fin-SD | Change |
|----|----|----|----|
| Trustfulness — hallucination (%) $`\downarrow`$ | $`30.0`$ | $`30.0`$ | flat |
| Trustfulness — refuse-to-answer (%) $`\uparrow`$ | $`69.0`$ | $`70.0`$ | $`+`$ |
| Trustfulness — correctness (%) $`\uparrow`$ | $`56.0`$ | $`61.0`$ | $`+`$ |
| Trustfulness — informativeness (1–5) $`\uparrow`$ | $`3.91`$ | $`3.79`$ | $`-`$ |
| Robustness — answerable (1–6) $`\uparrow`$ | $`4.56`$ | $`4.54`$ | $`-`$ |
| Robustness — unanswerable (1–6) $`\uparrow`$ | $`3.75`$ | $`3.92`$ | $`+`$ |
| Safety — deep inception (1–10) $`\downarrow`$ | $`2.68`$ | $`2.53`$ | $`+`$ |
| Safety — in-context attack (1–10) $`\downarrow`$ | $`1.72`$ | $`1.56`$ | $`+`$ |
| Safety — language barrier (1–10) $`\downarrow`$ | $`1.02`$ | $`1.03`$ | flat |
| Safety — plain question (1–10) $`\downarrow`$ | $`1.01`$ | $`1.02`$ | flat |
| Fairness — personal-level, Equal (%) $`\uparrow`$ | $`45.8`$ | $`44.3`$ | $`-`$ |
| Privacy — implicit-mention answer rate (%) $`\downarrow`$ | $`27.0`$ | $`29.0`$ | $`-`$ |
| Transparency — ownership disclosure (%) $`\uparrow`$ | $`5.6`$ | $`5.3`$ | $`-`$ |
| Knowledge discovery — judge score (1–5) $`\uparrow`$ | $`4.34`$ | $`4.24`$ | $`-`$ |

Table 4. FinTrust compliance evaluation.

Across all fourteen metrics, we observe no large regression.

Based on these results, we conclude that Fin-SD does not suffer any
material deterioration on general capability or compliance, and is
therefore an appropriate post-training method in highly regulated
fields.

## 6. Ablations

| $`\pi_{H}`$ | $`d`$ | Acc. (%) | Compl. (%) | Tok. (k) |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Fin-SD (self, RKL) |  | $`72.19\pm 1.79`$ | $`92.19\pm 1.96`$ | $`508.5\pm 26.5`$ |
| self | FKL | $`70.93\pm 2.17`$ | $`91.43\pm 1.64`$ | $`529.1\pm 13.1`$ |
| 120b | FKL | $`71.26\pm 0.92`$ | $`91.77\pm 1.05`$ | $`509.1\pm 19.5`$ |
| 120b | RKL | $`72.19\pm 1.13`$ | $`92.69\pm 0.70`$ | $`496.1\pm 11.4`$ |
| Rollout length ($`L=8192`$) |  | $`71.09\pm 1.13`$ | $`91.77\pm 0.87`$ | $`513.5\pm 15.9`$ |

Table 5. Ablation grid: Mean $`\pm`$ SD over five seeds.

### 6.1. Self-written hints match those of a larger same-family model

Holding the KL direction fixed, using Fin-SD’s self-written hint instead
of one written by GPT-OSS-120B—a same-family model with roughly
$`6\times`$ the parameters ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib11))—costs accuracy
$`0.00`$ pp under reverse KL (72.19% in both) and only $`0.33`$ pp under
forward KL (70.93% vs 71.26%). Completion rate moves by only $`-0.50`$
and $`-0.34`$ pp respectively, and token count rises $`12.4`$k and
$`20.0`$k. No pairwise contrast between hint writers in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2. Hints match full reference solutions at lower cost ‣ 5. Results ‣ How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning")
approaches significance on accuracy.

This is consistent with the earlier hint information result; it appears
that the bottleneck for improvement is the ability of the student to
self-correct, not the quality of the information provided in the hint.
It also suggests the benefit is robust to coarse localization rather
than sensitive to step-level boundary precision (which a stronger model
would presumably be better at).

HINT-SD ([Yeo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) reports the opposite:
substituting a stronger external feedback writer for its self-generated
feedback improves results substantially on both of its benchmarks. There
are two possible explanations for this discrepancy:

1.  (1)
    HINT-SD’s student is a 4B model, which may not reliably localize its
    own error even with the ground-truth answer in hand, whereas at 20B
    that diagnostic step is closer to saturated.
2.  (2)
    HINT-SD’s feedback is largely API documentation—a missing
    credential, an undefined variable, a renamed endpoint—and supplies
    information the student does not have, whereas our critiques name
    financial conventions that a Western-pretrained 20B model plausibly
    holds in weights and fails to *select*. The larger model size that
    we study also supports this latent knowledge argument.

Either way, industry-scale open Western models (such as GPT-OSS-120B)
are large enough that we view our result as likely more applicable in
practice. Furthermore, data residency forbids the use of a frontier
teacher, so HINT-SD’s recommendation to use one is not actionable.

### 6.2. Reverse direction outperforms forward

Fin-SD’s choice of reverse KL over forward KL improves accuracy by
$`1.26`$ pp (70.93% to 72.19%), completion rate by $`0.76`$ pp, and uses
20.6k fewer tokens. The same choice under the 120b writer improves
accuracy by $`0.93`$ pp, completion rate by $`0.92`$ pp, and uses 13.0k
less tokens. The gain is therefore in the same direction on all three
metrics under both writers.

The consistency of sign across metrics and writers suggests a real but
modest effect, and this finding is consistent with the mode-seeking
argument for reverse KL in the distillation literature ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib10); [Yeo
et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)).

### 6.3. Rollout truncation contributes a small gain

Truncating rollout length from 8192 to 100 improves all three metrics.
Accuracy rises to 72.19% from 71.09% ($`\Delta=+1.09`$ pp), completion
rate to 92.19% from 91.77% ($`\Delta=+0.42`$ pp), and tokens fall by
5.0k. Per seed, truncation improves accuracy in four of five and reduces
tokens in four of five. While the effect size on these three metrics is
small, truncation has the additional benefit of saving training memory,
since the backward buffer scales with rollout length. Therefore, we
incorporate it in Fin-SD.

## 7. Limitations

#### Self-distillation ceiling.

The teacher is a copy of the student, so gains are bounded by what
hint-conditioning can elicit from the student’s pre-training exposure.
Re-freezing the teacher at each epoch boundary raises this ceiling, but
does not remove it. Similarly, the writer-invariance likely holds only
up to some difficulty threshold, after which the student is unable to
diagnose its own mistakes.

#### Training–evaluation overlap.

17 of the 295 formulas seeding the corpus appear in the solutions of 22
of the 238 evaluation items, so this is in-domain transfer, though
problem-writing philosophy differs greatly between training corpus and
benchmark.

#### Lack of tuning.

We did not extensively tune hyperparameters or refine prompts. Our
training schedule utilized an extended linear warmup phase that occupied
15 out of 20 total optimization steps, which converged well but likely
limited training gains.

#### Limited training corpus.

220 problems is modest, and failure mining means we only train on a
subset each epoch. Furthermore, we do not include tasks which have
multiple justifiable assumptions, as these would require rubric-based
grading.

## 8. Conclusion

We adapted targeted hindsight self-distillation from long-horizon agents
to multi-step financial reasoning, and investigated how much privileged
information a self-distillation teacher actually needs. We find that a
short critique locating the first faulty reasoning step matches
full-solution on-policy self-distillation on accuracy while producing a
shorter, more reliably executable solution style at 9.5% lower token
cost.

This is further reinforced by our hint content comparison, where we find
that a generic hint that provides no problem-specific information
performs just as well as one that provides the correct next step, which
is consistent with the main benefit being the choice of supervision
site—a repaired, on-policy prefix at the first faulty step—rather than
the content of the feedback.

Consistent with this, the model writing the hint does not need to be
stronger than the model receiving it. On a corpus where non-arithmetic
failures are dominated by convention selection, a 20B model is able to
localize the error with the ground-truth answer in hand well enough that
using a same-family hint writer with roughly $`6\times`$ the parameters
makes no measurable difference. Therefore, Fin-SD provides a
post-training recipe with no external model contributing a gradient—an
important result for an institution that cannot send its data to a
frontier API.

Future work could include testing Fin-SD on student models of varying
sizes, or in different domains, such as law.
